abstract: |
  A study's protocol, experiment script, analysis pipeline, and publication figures begin as views of one design and drift apart as the study runs; by the end, no single artifact describes the study as it was actually run. Cognitive science has mature standards for its data (e.g., BIDS); the process that produces the data still lives in text, slides, and custom code. We present *Studyflow*, a visual notation that gives the experimental process a machine-readable, human-understandable, executable representation. A study is a typed directed graph, realized as an extension of the Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN 2.0) with the elements experimental research needs: domain-specific activities (cognitive task, questionnaire, instruction), decision gateways (randomization, eligibility), data operations, and data elements bound to community standards. One Studyflow file is at once the protocol, the runnable study, the analysis specification, and the publication figure, projected as multiple views for different audiences. We demonstrate one example of the notation end to end with a study in which human participants and a cohort of artificial agents perform the same cognitive tasks from one file, behind one execution interface. The example study provide a common protocol for asking where people and agents agree and where they diverge.
impact-statement: |
  A single machine-readable diagram serves as a study's protocol, runnable experiment, analysis specification, and publication figure for both human participants and artificial agents.

# Introduction

## The reproducibility gap is in *processes*, not just data

Every experiment accumulates documents that describe it, and by the end they disagree. A scientific experiment touches many people and systems: a researcher designs it; an ethics committee approves it; a participant runs it; a data pipeline ingests it; a model trains on it; a reviewer reads it as a manuscript; and a replicator tries to rebuild it. Reproducing it later requires more than the data and the manuscript: it requires an explicit, complete description of the *processes* that generated them [@aguilar2022experiments; @momeni2026guidelines]. In fact, a complete description of any computing system, including experiments, needs both a data model (for its structure and inputs/outputs) and a process model (for its behavior) [@olive2007conceptual].

In cognitive sciences, the processes behind the data are documented mainly in narrative prose, ad-hoc lab conventions, box-and-arrow diagrams, or code repositories that drift from the text they accompany [@bell2021perspectives; @osc2015; @nosek2022replicability]. The community has strong standards for the data, notably BIDS; the process, a record of how those data came to be, has no equivalent. The asymmetry has measurable consequences: even articles that share open data cannot be reproduced, because the process that connects the data to the results stays informal [@cruwell2023badge]. That asymmetry is the gap that we address in this paper.

The cost of this missing process model is clearest when someone other than the author re-reads a study. A battery of tasks, an online study on a recruitment dashboard, or an AI evaluation benchmark each accumulate the same trail: the protocol PDF, the ethics application, the experiment script, the preprocessing notebook, the model card [@mitchell2019modelcards], the manuscript figure, and the participant flow diagram; all begin as different views of the same study, and they end as inconsistent ones ([TODO: what does this mean;clarify:]some clinical studies, which add registries and acquisition pipelines, are the limiting case). By that point, no single artifact describes the study *as it was actually run*. Reviewers and replicators reach the code and data through these artifacts, so divergence among the artifacts limits how far the code and data can be independently checked. Trust in research is built or lost here.

The usual way to compensate for a missing process model is voluntary narrative reporting: checklists, preregistration forms, and journal endorsements. The available evidence suggests it has limited effect. [TODO: what is citation for this claim:] A cross sectional study of 400 psychology articles published in 2022 found that 7-14% had been preregistered and 14-16% shared raw data (the lower bounds from a broad sample, the upper from prominent journals). Despite more than a decade of data sharing and reproducibility reform [@hardwicke2024prevalence], gaps between endorsement and adherence recur across fields and journal policies [@percie2020arrive; @hair2019iicarus; @hardwicke2024transparency]. The reason is structural rather than a matter of researcher compliance: a checklist records *what to mention* without requiring *what to share*, and it accepts a narrative description of a process in place of a formal, verifiable one [@claesen2021adherence; @hardwicke2023preregistration]. AI evaluation has reached the same state: a benchmark is an experiment, and its results have proved sensitive to details of the procedure that no current artifact records [@burnell2023rethink; @biderman2024lessons]. Consequently, the underlying process model stays implicit and open to interpretation.

[TODO: Somewhere in this section mention even pre-registration is not a solution and imply that this is because as the studies are now complicated and dynamic and not everything is known per se]

We argue that reproducibility should be a property of the shared artifact itself, rather than separate documentation kept alongside the work. A single representation that is machine-readable, human-understandable, and shared across a study's many audiences would keep the process model and the data model aligned. [TODO: isn't this redundant? if yes, cleanup:] This paper's contribution is one version of that idea, built on a standard process notation.

## Related work

Today each audience of experimental research works with a different artifact, and these are hard to keep consistent. Existing approaches fall into a few overlapping families, none of which represents the whole experiment as one shared, executable artifact.

[TODO: in many places I've used experiment, study, experimental research, science, experimental sciences, etc. Make it more consistent and clarify if there are any differences in meaning intended. Also, in some places I've used "experiment" to refer to the process and in others to the data. Make this more consistent as well. The goal is to process-model the experiments in cognitive sciences; end-to-end]

**Workflow engines.** Scientists have long automated analysis with scripts and pipelines, and graphical platforms such as Galaxy [@thegalaxycommunity2024] and KNIME [@berthold2009] lowered the barrier to composing them. Modern engines model a process as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of tasks and orchestrate execution at scale, Nextflow [@nextflow] and Kedro [@kedro] among them, with NiPype and Pydra [@pydra] serving neuroimaging and workflow languages such as the Common Workflow Language [@cwl] making pipelines portable and declarative [@zhao2008scientific_workflows; @cuevasvicenttin2013workflows]. Within psychology, reproducible workflow practice wraps the analysis in code, containers, and build tools [@peikert2021reproducible]. These systems are powerful, but their representations target machines and developers, model the workflow as a DAG suited to fixed-input data pipelines, and encode study logic in code and configuration, as do continuous integration tools such as GitHub Actions [@kinsman2021] repurposed for scientific analysis. They demand programming skills that ethics boards, reviewers, domain experts, and many other collaborators do not have.

[TODO: cite snake in the previous paragraph]

**Experiment builders and orchestration platforms.** A separate ecosystem specifies and runs the behavioral experiment itself. Presentation libraries and builders implement tasks and studies: PsychoPy [@peirce2019psychopy], jsPsych [@deleeuw2015jspsych], lab.js with its structured JSON representation [@henninger2022labjs], OpenSesame, and the online Gorilla platform [@anwylirvine2020gorilla]. Above them, orchestration platforms run whole online studies: oTree [TODO: invalid ref: @chen2016otree] and Empirica [@almaatouq2021empirica] for interactive experiment designs, Dallinger and PsyNet for complex automated timelines [@harrison2026psynet], Pushkin for massive online cohorts [@hartshorne2019pushkin], and the Experiment Factory for containerized deployment of many cognitive tasks [@sochat2018expfactory]. A design layer is emerging as well: SweetPea compiles declarative factorial designs into stimulus sequences [@musslick2022sweetpea], AutoRA closes the loop between design, collection, and model discovery [@musslick2024autora], and SweetBean compiles one declarative stimulus specification to a jsPsych experiment for humans or a text experiment for language models [@strittmatter2025sweetbean]. Similarly, neuroscience has pushed furthest toward machine-readable task representation: BEADL specifies the state machine inside a single trial of a task in validated XML with a graphical editor and a Neurodata Without Borders binding [@beadl], and Bonsai [@lopes2015bonsai], pyControl [@akam2022pycontrol], and Autopilot [@saunders2019autopilot] [TODO: what does control rig mean? replace with something more clear]control rigs from formal task descriptions. Each of these specifies or runs one slice (a stimulus sequence, a state machine for single trials, a deployment) in code or a proprietary builder; none represents the whole study, from eligibility and allocation through analysis to the published figure, as one shared executable artifact.

**Protocol registries and guidelines.** Experimental protocols are shared as free-form text through registries such as protocols.io [@teytelman2016] or as manuscript supplements, and the EQUATOR network [@simera2010equator] catalogs reporting guidelines: CONSORT for randomized trials [@hopewell2025consort; @moher2012], SPIRIT for protocols [@spirit2013; @chan2025spirit], STROBE [@strobe], STARD [@stard], PRISMA [@page2021prisma], and TIDieR [@hoffmann2014tidier], several of which standardize flow diagrams [@egger2001]. These enforce structure only at the reporting stage, store it in free-form fields and proprietary formats such as PDF or DOCX, and yield no representation of the procedure that a machine can execute or verify. Executable publishing addresses the same problem from the publisher's side: eLife's Executable Research Articles make the analysis narrative live and runnable inside the published paper [@maciocci2019era; @tsang2020era], and hypothesis tests as code make the statistical prediction checkable [@lakens2021machinereadable], but the experimental procedure that produced the data still stays prose.

**Data standards and ontologies.** Community standards prescribe how datasets are organized: BIDS [@bids] and its extensions [@pernet2019eegbids], Psych-DS [@psychds], CSVW [@csvw], our Behaverse Data Model [@bdm], and the FAIR principles [@fair]. Adjacent efforts structure analysis outputs and methods reporting, NIDM-Results [@maumet2016nidm] and ARTEM-IS [@styles2021artemis; @soskic2025artemis], and process ontologies formalize semantics relevant to modeling workflow data [@norouzi2025semantic_processes]. All make the data or its products machine-readable but say little about the process that produced them.

**Provenance and packaging.** [TODO: Also mention reproducible envionments in coding like conda/pip/etc] The W3C PROV standard defines the vocabulary of provenance [@w3cprov], RO-Crate packages research artifacts with their metadata for FAIR exchange and archival [@soilandreyes2022rocrate], and Workflow Run RO-Crate records the provenance of computational workflow executions [@leo2024wfrunrocrate]; provenance systems such as Science Capsule [@ghoshal2021] record which software produced which output [@souza2020provenance], and process mining recovers models from runtime traces [@vanderaalst2016process]. All of these describe what was run retrospectively; none defines a prospective, executable of an experimental procedure for early steps of a study. They track the computation well but rarely the domain-specific experimental context: eligibility decisions, randomization, manual annotations (e.g., ICA labeling in EEG), protocol deviations, or the behavior of a participant [@simmons2018provenance_sport]. This paper's Studyflow aims to be complementary and provide a specification whose runs these standards can package (see Discussion).

**Visual notations.** Box-and-arrow figures communicate study logic at a glance but are not always standardized, rarely connected to the code, and usually tailored to one stakeholder: a CONSORT flow for a journal, a slide deck for a funding agency, a sketch for an engineer [@bogale2024]. Standardized graphical notations exist in adjacent fields, notably Systems Biology Graphical Notation [@novere2009], and BPMN [@bpmnspec] has been used for clinical pathways [@braun2014], serverless machine learning [@tetzlaff2022bpmn4sml], human and agent collaboration [@ait2024bpmn_humanagent], organizational modeling [@guerreiro2024], and process simulation [@cimino2025], with mature tooling (e.g., bpmn-js [@bpmnjs]), engines that generate executable code from diagrams [@diagrid], and recent large language model authoring tools (ProMoAI [@kourani2024promoai], conversational modeling [@kopke2025]) whose syntactic fluency does not by itself supply semantics or validation [@lauer2026assessing]. Dedicated efforts to document and visualize workflows for communication and publication point the same way [@willoughby2017], yet no such notation targets experimental cognitive science.

**Agents as participants.** Machine behavior research called for studying intelligent machines with the methods of behavioral science [@rahwan2019machine], and a fast-growing literature now administers psychology experiments to language models: cognitive task batteries [@binz2023gpt3; @codaforno2024cogbench], simulated human samples [@aher2023llms; @argyle2023silicon], human-versus-model comparisons on the same battery of tasks [@webb2023analogical; @strachan2024tom; @mei2024turing], and foundation models of cognition trained on human performance manually transcribed into text [@binz2025centaur], all under the banner of machine psychology [@hagendorff2024machinepsych]. In every one of these studies the protocol is a bespoke prompting harness re-implemented per paper, and human and model administration are matched by hand. Methodological critiques [@ivanova2025cognitive; @dillion2023replace; @lin2025fallacies] and a consensus reporting checklist for language model studies [@feuerriegel2026guidellm] now demand exactly what no current artifact provides: a pinned, shareable, executable record of how the experiment was administered.

**AI evaluation harnesses.** The same gap has been named inside AI evaluation. Shared harnesses standardize how models are scored, among them HELM [@liang2023helm], the LM Evaluation Harness [@biderman2024lessons], BIG-bench [@srivastava2023bigbench], and Inspect [@aisi2024inspect], onto which new evaluation frameworks are converging from earlier task specifications [@metr2024taskstandard]. Agentic benchmarks ship now the whole executable environments [@zhou2024webarena; @xie2024osworld; @mialon2024gaia]. Yet audits keep finding that what was run is unrecoverable from what was reported, and results shift with undocumented details of the experiments [@biderman2024lessons; @leech2024questionable], aggregate scores hide the behavior of single instances [@burnell2023rethink], and widely used benchmarks fail basic reproducibility criteria [@reuel2024betterbench; @kapoor2025agents]. These harnesses specify someyhing that only developers read and for machines only; none extends to a human subjects cohort, eligibility criteria, or publication figures. Consequently, where a benchmark reports a human baseline it is collected outside the benchmark artifact [@mialon2024gaia].

The drive toward machine-readable protocols is also not unique to cognitive and behavioral sciences. Clinical research is standardizing the protocol document itself, with CDISC ODM and its study design extension [@cdisc_odm], the ICH M11 structured digital protocol [@ich2025m11], and AI-specific reporting extensions of the guidelines mentioned above [@cruzrivera2020spiritai; @liu2020consortai]. In the wet lab, executable protocol languages such as Autoprotocol, LabOP, and Aquarium author log procedures from specification [@beal2022labop; @vasilev2021aquarium]; ISA-Tab structures experiment metadata for reuse [@sansone2012isa]; and psychology is formalizing the analysis plan as machine-readable preregistration [@peters2023preregr]. Each addresses a different dimension: the regulatory document, the reporting checklist, the lab procedure, the metadata record, or the analysis plan. None specifies an executable experiment in which the instrument is as diverse as a cognitive task and the subject may, unknowingly, be a person or an artificial agent.

Across these families the same limitations recur: (1) a representation is machine-facing or human-facing but rarely both; (2) experimental details stay informal during planning and execution; (3) [TODO: clarify this a bit and use simpler terms:] provenance stops at the computational boundary; (4) the experiment specifications that do exist cover only one task, one stimulus sequence, or one agent; and no artifact aligns the scientist, engineer, ethics board, funding agency, reviewer, and, increasingly, the AI evaluator. No single representation spans the full study lifecycle in a form that all of them can read, validate, and execute (Figure 1).

## Desiderata for a study specification language

A notation that closes the *process gap* (hence specify experimental studies) must satisfy several requirements at once: what the shared artifact *is*, how it behaves, who can read it, and how it stays grounded in existing standards. We state these requirements as seven desiderata. (R1), *a single source of truth*: one artifact serves every audience, so the views cannot drift apart. (R2) *Executable, not merely descriptive*: the specification runs; it does not only document. (R3) *Understandable to every audience without code*: an ethics board, a reviewer, or a collaborator can read it without programming. (R4) *Grounded in standards*: the artifact remains valid in a widely used standard notation and usable by generic tools that do not know the domain-specific extensions. R5, *process and data on one artifact*: the procedure and the data it produces are specified together. (R6) *Extensible without forking*: new domains and concepts plug in, not through changes to the core. (R7) *Execution agnostic*: who or what performs the protocol is a runtime decision, not a property of the specification. @tbl-requirements maps each desideratum to where the framework meets it.

## BPMN as a foundation

Meeting these desiderata is a language design problem. Experimental cognitive science meets the standard criteria for a domain-specific language (DSL): recurring structural patterns across studies, expert users who would benefit from a familiar notation rather than general purpose code, and no alternative executable language that already covers the whole experiment lifecycle [@mernik2005dsl]. Rather than invent a new notation, we extend an established one, because a notation that researchers, engineers, and reviewers already recognize is a cheaper starting point than a custom one.

Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) is a mature graphical language for processes, standardized by ISO [@white2004introduction]. It already provides what scientific workflows need (events, activities, sub-processes, gateways, data objects, sequence and data flows, and choreography), an established tooling ecosystem (`bpmn-js`, Camunda Modeler, and many tools for visualization), and a standard serialization, BPMN 2.0 XML, that engineers recognize and that outlives any single tool. When and why visual diagrams beat text is itself an empirical research topic [@moody2009physics; @larkin1987diagram; @figl2017comprehension].

We build on two of BPMN's extension mechanisms, `extensionElements` and namespaced attributes, which let authors add elements inside a new namespace that a generic BPMN parser ignores gracefully [@magnani2009bpdmn]. The same mechanism is used to extend the BPMN core in many other domains [@zarour2019; @braun2014classification]; experimental cognitive science is the gap they leave.

<!--
Recent large language model-assisted BPMN authoring tools (ProMoAI, BPMN-ChatBot, and related work [@kourani2024promoai; @kourani2024process_modeling_llm]) accelerate diagram authoring from text, but evaluations show that competitive syntactic quality does not translate into domain-specific semantics or domain-specific validation [@lauer2026assessing]. Authoring help is welcome; it is not a substitute for a profile that defines what *cognitive task*, *random assignment*, or *eligibility check* mean inside a process model. That profile is the gap Studyflow fills. -->

The rest of the paper is organized around the desiderata and our solution: the Studyflow notation meets the desiderata, the example study exercises them, and the discussion revisits where they hold and where they do not. The framework that follows delivers them as three artifacts: the notation itself, the multiple views it projects for different audiences, and open source reference toolkit that authors and runs studyflow diagrams. Together they make a study design tractable that current tooling cannot express in one artifact, e.g., enrolling human participants and a cohort of artificial agents in one identical, machine-readable, registrable protocol whose exported figure carries the protocol itself as its source data.

# The Studyflow framework

Each desideratum (@tbl-requirements) is met by a specific part of the framework, described below.

::: {#tbl-requirements .list-table header-rows=1 aligns="l,l" tbl-colwidths="[42,58]"}
The seven desiderata and where the framework meets each.

- - Desideratum
  - Where the framework meets it

- - R1 Single source of truth
  - One shared `.studyflow` source is at once the protocol, the runnable study, the analysis, and the figure (this section)

- - R2 Executable, not merely descriptive
  - The runner walks the same file a reviewer reads (the toolkit, below; semantics in Materials and methods)

- - R3 Legible to every audience without code
  - Four reader-facing views project from one source (multiple views, below)

- - R4 Grounded in standards, gracefully degrading
  - A valid BPMN 2.0 host with bindings to BIDS, Psych-DS, CSVW, and BDM (formal definition, below)

- - R5 Process and data on one canvas
  - Typed data, bound to schemas, joined to control flow by typed data-association edges (formal definition, below)

- - R6 Extensible without forking
  - A layered schema whose LinkML core is independent of any tool (formal definition and Materials and methods)

- - R7 Executor agnostic
  - One executor interface behind the runner, demonstrated end to end in Results
:::


## Formal definition

A Studyflow is a typed, attributed directed graph, a tuple $(N, E, T, \tau, \lambda)$. $N$ is a finite set of nodes: events, activities, gateways, actors, and data elements (datasets, schemas, stores), so the data plane lives inside the same object as the control flow. $E$ is a finite set of directed edges with endpoint maps $\mathrm{src}, \mathrm{tgt}: E \to N$, which admits parallel edges. $T$ is the set of node and edge types the language defines; $\tau: N \cup E \to T$ assigns each element its type, with sequence flow, message flow, and data association among the edge types. $\lambda$ attaches typed attributes to nodes and edges alike: the `instrument` of a cognitive task, the `probabilityFunction` of a random gateway, the `conditionExpression` of a guarded flow, or the `onset` and `duration` that drive the Gantt view. A versioned schema (below) fixes $T$ and the admissible attributes; a diagram is well-formed when its graph satisfies the structural constraints (every edge endpoint resolves, exactly one study root, a random gateway's branch probabilities sum to one, and, within the executable subset, every node that is not a gateway has at most one outgoing sequence flow) and its serialization conforms: valid BPMN 2.0 XML whose extension payload validates against a declared schema version. The graph is general rather than acyclic. Boundary events, message flows, and choreography express the interrupts, loops, and multi-party exchanges experimental procedures contain, which a directed acyclic graph represents only through external control logic. Everything that follows is grounded in this object; the four views are projections of it.

**A standard host notation.** Studyflow realizes this object as a domain-specific profile of BPMN 2.0 [@white2004introduction], tailored to experimental cognitive science. The diagrams stay valid BPMN 2.0 XML and open in any compliant tool (Camunda Modeler, bpmn.io, diagrams.net), and BPMN's extension mechanism (`extensionElements`, namespaced attributes) adds the domain semantics of $T$ and $\lambda$ without breaking the base standard [@stroppi2011; @magnani2009bpdmn].

**What Studyflow inherits.** Studyflow reuses BPMN's full vocabulary for control flow and structure: events (start, end, boundary, timer, error), activities (tasks, sub-processes, call activities), the five gateway types, sequence and message flows, data objects and stores with their associations, pools and lanes, and choreography for multi-agent interactions. These elements keep standard BPMN shapes and behave as the OMG specifies.

**What Studyflow adds.** Four areas extend BPMN with vocabulary experimental research routinely needs. First, a root **study container** groups every other element and carries metadata for the whole study (title, version, authors, runtime). Second, **domain-specific activity types** specialize the generic BPMN task with research-meaningful kinds (cognitive tasks, questionnaires, instructions, rest periods, video games, and a curated cognitive battery); each shows a distinctive icon but remains a normal BPMN task underneath. Third, **research-specific data elements** add bindings to community schemas (BIDS [@bids], Psych-DS [@psychds], CSVW) and our own Behaverse Data Model (BDM) [@bdm] on top of BPMN's generic data objects. A small **data operations vocabulary** (map, filter, flatMap, reduce, group, transform, compose) marks the *kind* of transformation on a task, so data flow is visible at a glance. Fourth, **research gateways** encode branching patterns specific to experimental design: a random gateway for randomization, a stratified allocation gateway, and an eligibility gateway that lists inclusion and exclusion criteria. Optional temporal attributes (onset, duration, progress) attach to activities and events, so the Gantt view derives trial schedules and visit calendars from the same diagram.

**What Studyflow deliberately leaves alone.** Studyflow leaves BPMN's serialization conventions, XML namespaces, element identifiers, and base shapes untouched; the domain extensions live inside BPMN's native extension slot, so a generic renderer ignores them gracefully while a validating tool reads and renders them.

**A layered set of schemas.** The vocabulary is split into a small core and optional domain extensions that load on demand (Figure 2); keeping the surface that always loads small is a choice backed by evidence, since comprehension of process models degrades with size and connector count [@reijers2011understandability]. The core covers the language scaffolding and a companion cognitive layer, while four optional layers cover specific domains: a cognitive assessment battery, generic process orchestration, data transformation at scale, and multimodal acquisition for EEG and eye tracking. New domains plug in by writing a schema, without changing the core. Supplementary Table S1 has the complete catalog; @tbl-elements gives a representative subset.

**A machine-readable specification.** The core language is defined by a versioned LinkML schema [@moxon2025linkml], mirrored by the runtime YAML schemas the BPMN tooling reads (Materials and methods). Listing 1 gives the schema for the study container and a cognitive task: a `CognitiveTask` specializes a generic data operation activity, requires an `instrument`, and carries an inline `configurations` block. Supplementary Listing S2 shows how a research gateway maps onto BPMN: a `RandomGateway` and an `EligibilityGateway` both specialize a standard `bpmn:ExclusiveGateway`, so they serialize and render as ordinary BPMN gateways while carrying the attributes that make randomization and eligibility explicit. The XML on disk appears where the worked example encodes its n-back task (Listing 2).

**Listing 1.** Studyflow language specification (LinkML excerpt; descriptions abridged). The schema fixes element types, required attributes, and validation rules independently of any tool.

```yaml
Study:
  class_uri: bpmn:Process
  tree_root: true
  attributes:
    name:
      range: string
      required: true
    version:
      range: string
    authors:
      range: string
      multivalued: true
    runtime:
      range: RuntimeEnum

CognitiveTask:
  is_a: DataOperationActivity        # a specialized BPMN activity
  class_uri: cognitive:CognitiveTask
  attributes:
    instrument:                      # psychopy, jspsych, labjs, ...
      range: string
      required: true
    configurations:                  # instrument-specific, inline YAML
      range: YAMLString
```


## Multiple views: Study, Gantt, Checklist, and Figure

Each view is a projection of the formal object: it keeps the nodes, edges, and attributes a given audience needs and drops the rest. The Gantt view, for instance, keeps the nodes whose $\lambda$ carries an `onset` or `duration` and lays them on a time axis, while the Study view sets those temporal attributes aside. Every view is a function of the single source and is never edited independently; the only state specific to a view, the Figure view's visibility flags, is itself stored in the source, so any two views of one file are consistent by construction. Projections are total (a study with no temporal attributes renders an empty Gantt) and lossy by design; the Figure export is the exception that restores everything, since the exported SVG embeds the complete source. A single `.studyflow` source therefore renders in four ways, each suited to a different stakeholder (Figure 5), and all four read the same file, so changes propagate automatically.

**Study view.** The default rendering is a BPMN-like graph that shows every element and connection. It is *structural*, showing what happens and in what order without committing to clock time, and it serves Methods sections, reviewers checking logical structure, and pipeline authors wiring up data flow.

**Gantt view.** A Gantt-style rendering places elements that carry timing along a time axis. BPMN has timer events but no native way to express activity duration, scheduled onset, or progress, so Studyflow attaches these as optional attributes on activities and events: **onset**, **duration**, and **progress** (percentage or label). Resource allocation uses BPMN pools and lanes directly to group rows, with no separate attribute. When the temporal attributes are present the view renders automatically, and the same mechanism scales from the timing of a trial (stimulus duration, ITI, response window) to the timing of a study (visit schedule, follow-ups), with milestones as elements with zero duration and hierarchical Gantts mapping onto sub-processes. It suits longitudinal studies and SPIRIT-style schedules of enrolment and assessment [@spirit2013].

**Checklist view.** This task-oriented view flattens the diagram into a list of activities (in topological order of the acyclic condensation of the sequence flow, document order within loops and ties) with their items and status, drawn from an optional `checklist` attribute (a markdown list) on every element. It supports two uses: *running studies day to day* (what is next, what is done) and *adhering to reporting guidelines* (CONSORT, SPIRIT, STROBE, PRISMA, and CARE), where guideline items map to the elements that satisfy them, so a study can be audited without leaving the diagram. Checklists ship inside the `.studyflow` file and export to JSON or Markdown for external task managers.

**Figure view.** The Figure view renders a diagram as a publication-ready SVG in which annotations on each element decide what is shown or hidden. A manuscript figure usually needs a curated subset of the full diagram, the protocol without the data layer or a single highlighted path through a branch, so rather than redraw by hand, an author marks elements to show or hide and exports the curated SVG. The exported SVG embeds the complete `.studyflow` source as metadata, so an author's own hosted or deposited figure is the runnable file itself rather than a picture of the study: a reader can lift the source back out, open it in the modeler, and re-run it. (Journal production pipelines typically re-encode figures and strip embedded metadata, so for published articles the same guarantee is delivered by shipping the `.studyflow` file as the figure's source data.) Because the visibility annotations live in the same `extensionElements` slot as the rest of the vocabulary, the figure stays valid BPMN and tied to the study it depicts. This is the mechanism behind the published CONSORT-style figure.

## The Studyflow toolkit: a modeler and a runner

Two open-source applications (MIT licensed and run in the browser) sit on top of the language: a modeler that authors diagrams and a runner that executes them. They are fully working prototypes rather than production software: reference implementations whose purpose is to show that the specification is authorable, executable, and machine-readable. Both are clients of the specification rather than owners of it. The core language stays a versioned LinkML schema [@moxon2025linkml] independent of either application, so third-party tools (linters, converters, and execution engines) can target the same specification, and each component, the schema, the modeler, the runner, and the data server that hosts published studies, evolves on its own while one `.studyflow` source ties them together.

**The modeler** authors, inspects, simulates, validates, and publishes diagrams (Figure 3), and its interface is generated from the schemas: the palette, the inspector, and the validation rules are all generated from the layered schemas (Materials and methods). A simulation mode steps through the diagram and runs the gateway logic, a soundness check that catches dead branches and missing conditions before a study runs [@dijkman2008semantics]. Export to PNG and SVG produces figures ready for publication whose SVGs embed the source XML. Publishing uploads the diagram to our data server [@bds], which builds its own participant interface from the diagram structure; each publish creates a new version on the server, so studies already in the field keep working when authors push updates.

**The runner** walks a participant or an artificial agent through a diagram node by node, reached from the modeler or directly by URL. It validates the diagram, traverses it from start to end rendering each node as a step, and applies any completion code or redirect at the end; a random seed makes branching deterministic (Materials and methods). It ships the step kinds the worked example needs (consent, instruction, questionnaire, cognitive task, and a generic fallback) and accepts new ones through a documented extension point, so a domain group can add a custom step without forking the runner. Its central design, one message passing executor interface behind which human and agent actors stand, drives the worked example in Results. The runner is above all a proof of concept that one `.studyflow` file is machine-readable and spans the use cases the language targets.

Authoring and running are fully client-side; the data server is needed only to host published studies and to serve the Behaverse assessment battery, and a task referenced by URL (a jsPsych or PsychoPy study, for example) runs without it. For third-party tools, conformance comes in three levels: a *rendering* tool (any generic BPMN application) opens the file and ignores the extensions (R4); a *validating* tool parses the extension namespaces and reports well-formedness against a declared schema version (R6); an *executing* tool implements the run semantics of the executable subset, preserving its determinism and amendment stability properties (Materials and methods) (R2).

A first study is a short exercise rather than a migration. The modeler runs in the browser without installation and ships the CONSORT 2025 and SPIRIT 2025 templates alongside the worked example; a reader can fork a template, rename its tasks, attach a consent document, and walk the result in the runner within minutes.

Figure 4 walks a participant from consent through an instruction, a questionnaire, and a cognitive task to the end screen, all on the same diagram authored above [FILL: runner screenshots from the seed-42 walkthrough].

# Results

This section follows one complete study from protocol to publication, showing that desiderata R1-R7 hold when a real study is run, not only described. We follow one human and agent agreement study, designed to registration standard, that exercises every part of the framework from a single file: nine people and a cohort of artificial agents perform the same six-task battery, allocated to a self-paced and a time-pressured path. It is a demonstration, not a finding about agents; the agent cohort table (@tbl-agents) and figures carry [FILL: values from the seed-42 runs] and show the shape of the result, not the result itself.

The same `.studyflow` file is the only input at every stage, design, enrollment, analysis, modeling, and reporting, so each stage reads or extends the artifact the stage before it left. The claim can be checked directly: the deposited file opens in the hosted modeler in any browser, with nothing to install, and loading it into the runner at study seed 42 walks the same battery reported here (Data availability).

## Design: a registrable agreement study of humans and agents

Our worked example asks an agreement question: across the six tasks of the battery, do people and agents reach approximate agreement, and where do they diverge? We operationalize agreement before the study runs, as part of the protocol (see the analysis stage below): per task, an equivalence test on accuracy with a prespecified margin, and a divergence readout, the discriminability of humans from each agent family by a classifier trained on the same trials, reported as the area under the curve against the empirical chance level. We give the study the full structure of a randomized controlled trial so the comparison is trustworthy before it runs. Each subject is allocated to one of two paths, self-paced and time-pressured, with task order drawn per subject from a balanced Latin square within each path [FILL: confirm the realized order scheme]. The timing manipulation binds differently per actor family (an enforced response window for humans and reinforcement learning agents, a deadline statement in the prompt for language models, a pondering budget for the recurrent model), so the path contrast is read within family rather than across the cohort. The protocol carries the scaffolding a registered study needs: consent, eligibility screening, seed-controlled random allocation to the two paths, and the structure a journal will later expect; the protocol file itself is deposited on OSF [FILL: registration DOI; state the deposit date relative to each arm's runs, and claim registration only for arms run after it], so the registered artifact and the executed artifact are one file; the registration identifier is in turn written onto the study container before deposit [FILL: confirm], so the file names its own registration.

In current practice this scaffolding is spread across a registry entry, an ethics PDF, a recruitment system, and a CONSORT flow diagram drawn at write-up time, none of them a machine-readable view of the others [@moher2012; @rennie2001; @hopewell2025consort]. The flow diagram, in particular, is a participant-tracking schematic; its four standard rows are enrollment, allocation, follow-up, and analysis, and attrition counts annotate each transition. It is a *document* about the trial rather than the *spec* that drove it.

We start from the CONSORT 2025 reference diagram that ships with the modeler; authors can fork it, parameterize it, and run it as the actual protocol of a new trial [@hopewell2025consort]. Figure 6 compares three artifacts: (a) the standard CONSORT 2025 reference flow as published by the CONSORT group, (b) a Studyflow reproduction encoded with the same labels and pathways, and (c) an annotated comparison whose left path uses Studyflow boundary error events and whose right path uses the traditional text and box treatment.

The key mechanical difference is how attrition is represented. In the traditional figure, each "Excluded / Did not receive / Lost to follow-up / Discontinued" box is an unconnected annotation that sits next to the column of follow-up activities, and readers must infer that these counts subtract from the main flow. In the Studyflow diagram, attrition is encoded as a *boundary error event* attached to the activity that participants left from. Exclusion at screening hangs off the eligibility gateway, non-receipt of intervention off the two allocation tasks, loss to follow-up and discontinuation off the follow-up tasks, and exclusion from analysis off the analysis tasks. Each event ends in an error end event that carries the count as a typed attribute, with the display label derived from it. This has three consequences. First, the diagram's topology now matches the trial's topology, so a participant lost during follow-up exits along an edge that starts at the follow-up activity itself, rather than an arrow drawn from a side annotation. Second, the flow arithmetic becomes a conservation law: at every activity, inflow equals outflow plus attrition. The runner writes realized counts onto activities and attrition counts onto the error end events, and the validator checks the law over the whole figure, sums that in a published CONSORT diagram are added by hand and checked by eye. Third, the boundary error event is the same primitive that BPMN uses to model interrupts in any business process, so the diagram stays valid BPMN 2.0 and inherits the standard execution semantics for error handling [@bpmnspec; @dijkman2008semantics].

In the file, each attrition path is a few lines of standard BPMN: a boundary error event wired to an error end event whose count is a typed attribute, with the label derived from it:

```xml
<bpmn2:boundaryEvent id="Dropout" attachedToRef="Battery">
  <bpmn2:outgoing>Flow_Dropout_Excluded</bpmn2:outgoing>
  <bpmn2:errorEventDefinition id="ErrorDef_Dropout" />
</bpmn2:boundaryEvent>
<bpmn2:endEvent id="Dropout_End" name="Dropped out (n=...)">
  <bpmn2:extensionElements>
    <studyflow:attrition count="..." />
  </bpmn2:extensionElements>
  <bpmn2:errorEventDefinition errorRef="ErrorDef_Dropout" />
</bpmn2:endEvent>
```

The diagram carries domain semantics alongside the BPMN structure. The enrollment start event references the consent PDF participants see, so a runner reaching this node renders the consent screen before any randomization. The screening task carries a markdown checklist that drives the Checklist view (the demographic intake, medical history, and baseline screen items shown are the CONSORT reference template's; the demonstration study collected demographics only); the eligibility and randomization gateways are typed as such; each battery task declares itself a cognitive task with its own inline parameter block (for the n-back: the N level, stimulus duration, inter-trial interval, and trials per block); and the allocation, follow-up, and analysis tasks carry checklists describing protocol obligations. A single file therefore serves four readers at once: the registry (a registrable protocol with explicit randomization and eligibility criteria), the ethics board (consent content and the checklists on each task), the data collection platform (the embedded cognitive-task instrument and its parameters), and the journal (the CONSORT figure with attrition flows already wired) [@stroppi2011]. The union of those layers, rendered together, *is* a CONSORT diagram.

Where CONSORT structures the *report*, SPIRIT structures the *plan*. The same study also renders as a SPIRIT 2025 schedule of enrolment and assessment, its checklist items mapping onto the Gantt view from a worked template the modeler ships [@chan2025spirit; @spirit2013]. A SPIRIT plan and a CONSORT report are then the same file at two points in its lifecycle: the schedule before randomization, and the flow diagram with attrition counts written into the labels of the boundary error events once the study has run.

The same flow enrolls, allocates, follows up, and analyzes an agent exactly where it does a person, because the executor is a runtime choice (next subsection). CONSORT and SPIRIT originate in human trials, and reading agents as co-subjects in one flow is a deliberate extension the unified representation makes natural, in the spirit of studying machine behavior with the methods of behavioral science [@rahwan2019machine]. *Co-subject* is a notational term throughout: both kinds of actor traverse the same enroll, allocate, run, and analyze topology and write to one table; it implies no ethical or inferential standing for the agents (see Discussion). A run that exceeds its failure threshold leaves the study along the same edge a participant lost to follow-up does.

## Enroll and run: one diagram runs the study for every subject

This stage runs both kinds of co-subject through one diagram, making Studyflow's central idea concrete: *who executes the protocol is a runtime decision, not a property of the diagram*. Participants and agents traverse the identical enroll, allocate, run, and analyze topology and write into one shared table that validates against the trials schema.

**The battery.** Our study administers a six-task Behaverse battery: tasks conventionally associated with working memory (n-back [@owen2005nback; @redick2013nback] and digit span [@richardson2007span]), attention (multiple-object tracking [@pylyshyn1988mot]), processing speed (pattern comparison [@salthouse1991speed]), fluid reasoning (matrix reasoning [@raven2000matrices]), and set-shifting (card sorting [@grant1948sorting]). Task and construct variance are confounded here: most labels carry a single task, and the one label with two, working memory, pairs n-back with digit span, the canonical example of weak convergent validity [@redick2013nback]; people and agents are therefore compared at the task level throughout; the construct words name lineages, not measurement claims. One `.studyflow` source drives every task and actor; each task runs [FILL: trials per task] trials per subject. The n-back serves as the worked example below, and the other five use the same machinery.

**The round-trip: enroll, allocate, and follow up.** We built the battery in the modeler as one diagram that orchestrates the four CONSORT stages for both paths: enrollment through consent and baseline questionnaires, an eligibility gateway, randomized allocation to the self-paced and time-pressured paths, and follow-up through the six tasks. Each task is itself a nested timeline of blocks (a warm-up, the test blocks, and any adaptive staircase) that prose and slides flatten but the diagram keeps explicit; warm-up exposure is identical for human and agent subjects. Loaded into the runner, the diagram is checked for required parameters and then walked one node at a time (Figure 4). Randomness follows a two-level seed policy: the study seed (42 for every run reported here) combines with the subject identifier to fix that subject's path, task order, stimulus order, and every random branch, while responses stay sampled, not seeded (Materials and methods). Each agent cell therefore runs [FILL: k] times under recorded sampling parameters and is reported aggregated over runs, with dispersion rather than a single canonical trace.

**Encoding the trials.** Figure 7 places the traditional slide version of the n-back figure next to the Studyflow equivalent. The slide is intuitive but underspecified: timing values often live only in the caption, the boundary between trial and block stays implicit, and decisions like "what counts as a correct match" are buried in the analysis code. Studyflow instead encodes the trial as an explicit subgraph: a stimulus activity, a boundary timer for the response window, a second for the inter-trial interval, and annotations labeling the target and non-target branches. The trial-by-trial encoding in Figure 7 is illustrative; for runs beyond a handful of trials the same logic compresses into a single cognitive task whose inline configuration declares the N level, stream, trial count, stimulus duration, and inter-trial interval, which the runner expands into individual trials (Listing 2, abridged). The same compression applies to every task in the battery. Each trial is logged to our trials schema (BDM [@bdm], Psych-DS-compatible [@psychds]), so the same diagram produces a CSV whose columns the schema fixes and whose meaning the diagram fixes, identically across all six tasks; a third party with only those two files can reconstruct what each row means without the modeler. Releasing results at the level of single instances, which reformers ask AI evaluation to adopt [@burnell2023rethink], is here the default output rather than a supplementary courtesy.

**Listing 2.** The n-back task serialized in a `.studyflow` file (BPMN 2.0 XML, abridged; the stimulus stream is truncated for display). The task is a standard `bpmn:task` carrying a `cognitive:task` extension; its inline `cognitive:configurations` block declares the N level, the stimulus stream, and the timing.

```xml
<bpmn2:task id="Task_NB" name="N-back (digits)">
  <bpmn2:extensionElements>
    <cognitive:task scene="NB" configMode="inline">
      <cognitive:configurations>
        NValue: 2
        Feature: Digits
        Streams:
          - StimulusValue: [3, 1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3, 1]
        StreamSize: 12
        StimulusDisplayDuration: 0.5
        InterStimulusInterval: 1.5
      </cognitive:configurations>
    </cognitive:task>
  </bpmn2:extensionElements>
  <bpmn2:incoming>Flow_B_Start_NB</bpmn2:incoming>
  <bpmn2:outgoing>Flow_NB_DS</bpmn2:outgoing>
</bpmn2:task>
```

**One executor, many actors.** Behind the runner stands one abstraction: an actor is anything that maps a trial's observation to a response. The runner administers every actor through one message passing interface built on exactly that exchange (Figure 8). Per trial it sends the stimulus, the allowed responses, the timing constraint, and where needed a rendered frame, and records the response and, where applicable, the response time under the common schema. Each actor keeps its own state behind that interface, a participant's session, an agent's policy, a recurrent hidden state, or a language model's context, so the runner never reaches inside it; human and agent co-subjects are actors in one shared space. Each realizes an Actor element the language types by `actorType` (human, LLM, agent, or instrument), and this study fills the executor with four kinds of actor.

The *human* actor renders each trial in the interface participants see and blocks until a person responds; nine participants ran the battery this way, a sample sized for the demonstration rather than for human inference between the arms (Materials and methods). *Reinforcement-learning agents* run through CogEnv [@ansarinia2022cogenv], which drives RL policies through the bot interface the Behaverse assessment application exposes, so an agent meets the same stimuli, response options, and time constraints a participant does; a random or scripted policy also validates the protocol, surfacing stuck states and timing edge cases before any human sits down. *Recurrent cognitive models* run through CogPonder [@ansarinia2023cogponder], our differentiable PonderNet-based model that reproduces human accuracy and response times by controlling its pondering steps before committing; it returns both a response and a response time predicted by the model, so the cohort gains a process model whose latencies are predicted from the task, not sampled from a prompt. *Language model agents* run through a package that sends each trial to the configured model with a versioned trait prompt (below); models with vision input also read the rendered frame, a necessity the visual-cognition literature independently motivates, since vision-language models show systematic deficits on exactly the low- and mid-level visual tests the battery's spatial tasks (object tracking, matrix reasoning, card sorting) probe [@schulzebuschoff2025visual; @tangtartharakul2026deficits], where earlier comparisons had to hand-translate such stimuli into text [@webb2023analogical]. Response time is interpretable only where the actor produces it as behavior: measured for humans, predicted by the model for the recurrent family; reinforcement learning agents yield environment step latency and language models yield elapsed latency, both logged as infrastructure metadata and excluded from any latency analysis (@tbl-agents marks RT provenance per family).

If an actor replies outside the allowed set, the runner records the raw reply and flags the trial as missing; no response is imputed. A prespecified rule on whole runs turns persistent failure into attrition: a run whose rate of flagged trials exceeds [FILL: threshold]% on any task exits through the boundary error event and is counted in the participant flow, so agent dropout flows along the same edge as human loss to follow-up. Flagged trials are typed by failure mode (refusal, parse failure, timeout), reported per cell in @tbl-agents. Instantiating an executor package is the agent's enrollment record, with model identity, version, and sampling parameters pinned to every run (Materials and methods); published guidance on administering cognitive evaluations to language models asks for exactly these records [@ivanova2025cognitive; @lampinen2024content], and the artifact makes them checkable properties rather than narrative compliance.

**The agent cohort: a matrix enrolled across the battery.** We enroll a matrix of agents across the whole battery, rather than scoring one agent on one task, so the agents meet the same six tasks the people traverse. We cross three factors within each allocation path. The first is *model*: a uniform random baseline, a recurrent cognitive model (CogPonder), a reinforcement learning policy through CogEnv, several open-weight text models served locally through Ollama (pinned by content digest and quantization), and a commercial vision-language model (Claude, pinned by snapshot identifier). The second is *trait*: targeted response profiles from prior characterizations of human participants, a "careful" profile with the conservative decision criterion the diffusion model formalizes [@ratcliff2008diffusion], a "fatigued" profile marked by intermittent attentional lapses [@robertson1997oops], and a profile at the fast, error prone end of the classic trade between speed and accuracy [@wickelgren1977sat]. Trait names denote the response profile the manipulation targets, not an internal state of the model, and the manipulation is family-specific: a versioned persona prompt for language models (the silicon-sampling method applied to performance profiles rather than demographics [@argyle2023silicon; @aher2023llms]), the pondering cost for the recurrent model, the policy for the reinforcement learning agent; trait effects are therefore analyzed within family, not across. Trait prompts describe a disposition only and never name a target accuracy or error rate, so the agreement estimate is not steered toward its own outcome; the prompts ship as versioned artifacts referenced from the diagram. The third factor is *task*: the six battery tasks. Each model also runs a default cell with no trait prompt, and the headline equivalence tests read off that cell; trait cells are analyzed as manipulations within family. Agents are enrolled exhaustively, [FILL: k] distinct subject identifiers per cell within each path at study seed 42: a factorial sweep rather than a randomized allocation, so the CONSORT allocation row applies to the human arm alone. @tbl-agents reports accuracy, the rate of flagged trials by failure mode, and response time where provenance permits, for every cell [FILL: values from the seed-42 runs], and Figure 9 shows the profiles across tasks against the human reference band [FILL: rendered from the same runs]; the random baseline sits near chance, and the open-weight models run the same battery without an external API [FILL: the observed open- versus closed-weight pattern]. This is the "few models, many items" regime [@ansarinia2022cogenv] extended across tasks: rather than rank many models on a single task, a choice that itself moves rankings [@dehghani2021lottery], we vary the diagram (task, response window, trait) and profile a cohort of agents over a battery of parametrically related items, the construct-profiling design the AI evaluation literature has begun to call for [@wang2026psychometrics; @bean2025construct]. The nearest existing artifacts make the differentiation concrete: CogBench scores many language models on seven fixed paradigms behind one code harness [@codaforno2024cogbench], and Psych-101 hand-transcribes 160 experiments into text to train Centaur [@binz2025centaur]; here the protocol itself is the shared executable artifact, so human and agent administration are identical by construction, and the battery re-parameterizes from the diagram rather than the harness.

::: {#tbl-agents .list-table header-rows=1 aligns="l,l,l,r,r,r,l" tbl-colwidths="[14,14,14,12,16,14,16]"}

RT provenance is marked per family (predicted by the model for the recurrent family; environment step latency for reinforcement learning agents and elapsed latency for language models, both excluded from latency analyses; the human reference values appear in Figure 9). The full crossing is in the supplementary table; this table summarizes per family.

**Beyond one participant.** The notation already expresses interaction itself as the unit: BPMN 2.0's **choreography task** models a directed exchange with an explicit initiator [@pufahl2022; @decker2011choreography], a choreography task between a human and an LLM agent is the same primitive as one between two humans, and the diagram validates against the BPMN 2.0 choreography schema even though the runner does not yet traverse it (see Limitations) [@stroppi2011].

## Measure agreement: human and agent comparison and the CONSORT flow

Because both kinds of subject wrote to one shared table with a declared schema, this stage reads the agreement question off that table and closes the CONSORT flow by counting the analysis exclusions on the same record. The analysis that produces this readout is usually a script, an R or Python notebook whose structure (the order of operations, their dependencies, the kind of each step) lives in code and comments rather than in a machine-readable record. Studyflow's data operations give every operation an explicit type (map, filter, flatMap, reduce, group, transform, compose), so the *kind* of work each step does is visible in the diagram.

We analyze the trials through a typed pipeline: read the raw trials; filter invalid ones (RT < 100 ms, missing data, flagged rows), which is the analysis exclusion row of the CONSORT flow, applying one rule set to both populations so a failed human trial and a flagged agent trial are removed at the same node and counted together; map to derived measures; branch at an exclusive gateway on the comparison of interest; reduce in two stages, first to summaries for each subject (or each run) and then to group-level statistics, so the uncertainty respects the clustering of trials within subjects; route through a manual review of outliers; and render and write the summary table and figures, each to a dataset with a declared schema. The agreement estimand declared in the design stage is encoded here as typed analysis nodes: per task, an equivalence test on accuracy whose margin and alpha are attributes of the node [FILL: margins, justified from test-retest variability of the battery], and an item-level readout, the correlation of per-item accuracy profiles between cohorts. At nine humans these margins are necessarily wide; the human arm demonstrates the mechanism, and the agent cohort, where runs are cheap, carries any substantive read. The prespecified test is therefore an element of the registered file rather than a paragraph beside it: the registered analysis and the executed analysis are the same node, and any divergence between them is a diff, not a reading. Three properties are not optional: the conditional branch is visible in the topology rather than buried inside an `if`; the manual review has an explicit place in the diagram, making it harder to skip; and the schema on the output table is part of the spec rather than implicit in the column names.

Because the same diagram carries process and typed data together, the human and agent agreement is auditable from one artifact rather than asserted across mismatched ones. Activities sit on the sequence-flow graph, while datasets, stores, catalogs, schemas, and snapshots sit on a parallel data-flow graph that BPMN data associations, drawn as dashed edges, connect. Every dataset declares its format (BDM, BIDS, Psych-DS, or generic) and a schema, inline or external; tabular data carries a CSVW body or a schema reference [@hoytO3GuidelinesOpen2024; @csvw], while non-tabular data documents tensor dimensions, dtypes, and units. Bindings to BIDS [@bids], Psych-DS [@psychds], and BDM [@bdm] are typed contracts that the modeler validates and the runner respects, so an analyst can confirm from the diagram alone that a downstream task consumes exactly the column an upstream task produced.

Concretely, Figure 10 shows the RT analysis subprocess beside the equivalent dplyr code. The diagram encodes the same chained pipeline a tidyverse user would write as `filter |> mutate |> group_by |> summarize`, but it adds two commitments. First, the inputs and outputs are typed (BDM trials level in, models level out), registered in a catalog, and physically stored in a backing store (a ducklake of DuckDB and Parquet in our example). Second, the analysis task's composed-operation marker declares which primitive operations the task may perform, so tooling can reject any implementation that touches an undeclared column or runs an unauthorized operation.

Preregistration of analysis then becomes the diagram itself. In current practice a preregistered plan is free text on a registry website, with no link a machine can check to the code that is eventually run; preregistered studies routinely deviate without disclosure [@claesen2021adherence; @hardwicke2023preregistration], a prominent replicability demonstration was retracted after its analyses were found not to match its own registration [@bakcoleman2024rigour], and tooling now uses language models to approximate the registration-to-paper comparison post hoc [@cummins2026regcheck]. Machine-readable hypothesis tests made the statistical plane of this problem checkable [@lakens2021machinereadable], and structured preregistration made the plan itself machine-readable [@peters2023preregr]; under the Studyflow encoding the same logic extends to the whole process: the diagram is the spec, the dplyr pipeline is one valid implementation, and any divergence between the two shows up in the data operation markers and the input and output schemas as a graph diff rather than a prose comparison. The modeler reduces visual density with collapsible layers, turning the data layer off for the high-level protocol and on for the full dependency graph.

The worked dataset is the seed-42 agent cohort and the human battery of nine participants, both written to the same trials schema [FILL: summary RT values and per-task agreement once the analysis is run].

## Model agreement: a human versus agent classifier

The analysis stage reads agreement off group summaries, and the same trials feed a model that learns the divergence readout declared in the design: a classifier separating humans from each agent family in turn, whose discriminability per task locates where the populations separate. Performance at the empirical chance level operationalizes indistinguishability, complementing the equivalence tests of the analysis stage; cross-validation is grouped so that all trials of a subject (or of an agent run) fall in the same fold, the uniform random baseline is excluded from these comparisons, and the input features are restricted to fields defined for every compared family (responses and accuracy, not latency). The same machinery extends to a model of the response time distribution for the actor families whose latencies are interpretable, or, with neural recordings, a multimodal predictor. Because both cohorts wrote one shared table, the classifier trains on the same rows the comparison reads and is authored in the same diagram rather than a separate codebase. ML pipelines suffer the same fragmentation as experimental protocols [@kapoor2023leakage], with the model card [@mitchell2019modelcards], feature engineering, training script, deployment config, and retraining triggers scattered across repositories and cron jobs; Studyflow's data operations, gateways, and data elements bound to schemas apply to them as cleanly as to behavioral analyses, so an analysis and a training pipeline share one notation with different operators [@tetzlaff2022bpmn4sml].

Beyond the classifier, the same notation expresses a full multimodal preprocessing and training pipeline that harmonizes EEG and behavioral recordings across heterogeneous public datasets, which we specify in Supplementary Figure S1 rather than run here: provenance is the diagram, the analytical multiverse is explicit branches rather than forks under version control [@steegen2016multiverse], and a preprocessing subprocess defined once applies to every dataset in the same format [@tetzlaff2022bpmn4sml; @ghosh2025reproducible_digital_health].

## Report: the file that ran the study is the CONSORT figure and the benchmark

The lifecycle closes where it began, with the reporting guidelines that shaped the design. Because the study ran inside the same file, the CONSORT figure is not redrawn at write-up time; the modeler's Figure view exports it from the protocol that enrolled, allocated, followed up, and analyzed both cohorts, with the attrition counts already written into the boundary error events. The exported source is at once the CONSORT report and the specification of the agreement benchmark it ran; the figure's source-data file in this article is that runnable file, and the diff between the registered protocol and the file as run consists of the attrition counts alone; Listing 3 shows that diff in full.

**Listing 3.** The complete deviation report of the worked study: the diff between the `.studyflow` file deposited at registration and the same file after the run (study seed 42). Every changed line is a count the runner wrote, or a label derived from one; the protocol's topology, parameters, and seeds are untouched. [FILL: replace the block below with the verbatim output of `git diff --no-index` between the OSF deposit and the file as run.]

```diff
--- registered.studyflow
+++ as_run.studyflow
-  <bpmn2:endEvent id="Dropout_End" name="Dropped out (n=...)">
+  <bpmn2:endEvent id="Dropout_End" name="Dropped out (n=[FILL])">
     <bpmn2:extensionElements>
-      <studyflow:attrition count="" />
+      <studyflow:attrition count="[FILL]" />
```

Reporting against a guideline then becomes a property the diagram can be checked for, rather than a PDF assembled alongside it. Each guideline is, in structure, a controlled vocabulary, a checklist, and sometimes a flow diagram, and Studyflow handles all of them the same way: checklist items become entries in the optional `checklist` attribute, flow diagrams become Studyflow renderings with boundary error events for attrition, and vocabulary becomes labels on activities, gateways, and data elements. Items without structural counterparts (harms, blinding, sample-size rationale) map to checklist markdown on elements rather than to topology. Because the checklist attribute is machine-readable, the Checklist view shows the items as a markdown list, each linked back to the element that satisfies it; the view supports the audit but does not replace it, and a human board or editor still decides conformance. The EQUATOR network catalogs these standards [@simera2010equator]; Supplementary Table S2 lists the most widely used, with Studyflow's current coverage. The two templates that ship today (CONSORT 2025, whose 30-item checklist [@hopewell2025consort] maps onto the shipped template, and SPIRIT 2025, whose 34 items map onto the Gantt view as both schedule and checklist [@chan2025spirit], Figure 11) exercise the full mechanism; the entries marked Roadmap are authoring work rather than missing capability, since the elements, attributes, and Checklist view they need are already in place.


The pattern recurs across the catalog, with STROBE and PRISMA next: PRISMA 2020 [@page2021prisma] standardized the study flow diagrams that are visual instances of what Studyflow generalizes, TIDieR [@hoffmann2014tidier] makes intervention details explicit items that map onto the participant branch, and ARRIVE 2.0 [@percie2020arrive], with its history of endorsement without adherence, supplies the animal-research counterpart. The newest entry is telling: a consensus reporting checklist for language model studies in behavioral science now exists [@feuerriegel2026guidellm], and the worked study already records its core items (model identity, version, prompts, sampling parameters, failure handling) machine-readably. The benchmark literature is converging on the same form from the other side: benchmark-quality checklists [@reuel2024betterbench; @zhu2025abc] are, in structure, EQUATOR-style reporting guidelines, and they map onto the Checklist view exactly as CONSORT items do.

Reporting guidelines and execution specifications need not be different artifacts. At publication, the manuscript ships three artifacts that are all views of one source: the exported figure (CONSORT report and benchmark specification), the Checklist view audit against the target guideline, and the `.studyflow` file itself, paired with the shared trials table that holds both subject populations. From these, a reader can reconstruct what every element and every column means, and read where the people and the agents agree across the battery and where they diverge, without rerunning the study.
