# Discussion

## What Studyflow changes: from divergent artifacts to one auditable diagram

Current practice keeps the *protocol*, the *code*, and the *figure* as three separate artifacts that begin in agreement and drift apart over a project's life. Studyflow consolidates them into one file, the single source of truth: the same CONSORT diagram is the participant flow figure, the spec a reviewer audits, and the artifact the data collection application steps through, so the views can no longer drift apart. That source is plain XML, so it diffs in Git and embeds in image metadata, bringing procedural specifications under the version control discipline that already governs data and code.

Because one protocol serves many actors, a human and agent agreement study becomes one auditable artifact. The same source runs human participants and artificial agents behind one execution interface, and the worked example uses this to author a study in which people and a cohort of artificial agents are co-subjects, in the notational sense defined above. This supplies the standardized, auditable, multi-executor evaluation protocol that agreement-based analyses presuppose on the measurement side [@nayebi2026alignment]: a fixed task space (here six cognitive tasks, not safety values), one executable protocol, and one record, under one schema, for every actor. For AI evaluation the artifact sits in a recognizable lineage: model cards and datasheets document models and data [@mitchell2019modelcards; @gebru2021datasheets], and evaluation cards have been proposed for evaluations themselves [@dhar2025evalcards]; a `.studyflow` benchmark is, in those terms, an eval card a third party can execute, at a moment when audits find most benchmarks underdocumented and hard to rerun [@reuel2024betterbench; @kapoor2025agents]. A benchmark no longer needs to be written three times in three formats, and, unlike existing agentic benchmarks whose human baselines are collected outside the benchmark artifact [@mialon2024gaia], here the human and agent cohorts are enrolled, allocated, excluded, and analyzed through the same file.

One property underlies them all, the one promised in the Introduction and exercised by the worked study: reproducibility becomes a feature of the shared artifact, not of documentation kept beside it.

## Relationship to existing ecosystems

Studyflow sits at the intersection of several ecosystems, and it does not aim to replace any of them.

**Workflow engines and evaluation harnesses.** A family of engines solves a problem Studyflow leaves alone: scalable, reproducible execution on heterogeneous compute, among them Nextflow, the Common Workflow Language (CWL), the Workflow Description Language (WDL), Pegasus, Apache Airflow, Kedro, NiPype, and Pydra [@zhao2008scientific_workflows; @cuevasvicenttin2013workflows; @nextflow; @cwl; @pydra]. The two are complementary: where a DAG fits data pipelines with fixed inputs and outputs, Studyflow sits *above* such systems, since a task can reference an external script (a Nextflow process, a Kedro node, a NiPype workflow) and a downstream tool can compile the protocol diagram into an executable graph [e.g., @ghosh2025reproducible_digital_health]. The same complementarity holds for AI evaluation harnesses [@aisi2024inspect; @biderman2024lessons]: an Inspect task or an lm-eval run is one valid executor behind the runner interface (R7), and the Studyflow file is the protocol it implements. By the same logic, Studyflow leaves process mining to other tools, which can consume its traces directly [@vanderaalst2016process].

**Experiment builders and task specification languages.** SweetBean compiles one stimulus specification to a human or a language model experiment [@strittmatter2025sweetbean], Deliberate Lab runs language model agents as first-class participants alongside humans in real-time group experiments [@tessler2025deliberatelab], and BEADL specifies the state machine inside a single task trial in validated XML [@beadl]; these are the closest existing artifacts to parts of Studyflow, and several are more expressive on their own slice (constraint-solved factorial sampling in SweetPea [@musslick2022sweetpea], adaptive closed-loop designs in AutoRA and PsyNet [@musslick2024autora; @harrison2026psynet], real-time multiplayer in Empirica [@almaatouq2021empirica]). The differentiation is scope and lifecycle: each specifies a stimulus sequence, the state machine of a trial, or a runtime platform, in code or a bespoke format; Studyflow extends an ISO-standard general notation, spans eligibility, allocation, analysis, and reporting, binds to human-science data and reporting standards, and abstracts over four actor families rather than language models alone. A Studyflow cognitive task can carry a SweetPea-generated sequence; the layers compose. Adoption likewise does not ask a lab to rewrite the task it already has: a jsPsych or PsychoPy task referenced by URL becomes the `instrument` of a cognitive task, and the diagram supplies what currently lives around that task in separate documents, the consent, the eligibility rule, the allocation, the data contract, and the figure. For human participants this path runs today; the agent adapters need a per-task bridge (see Limitations).

**Data standards.** BIDS, BDM, Psych-DS, and CSVW prescribe how datasets are structured [@bids; @bdm; @psychds; @csvw]; Studyflow describes the process that produced them and references these standards through dataset, table, and schema elements: a BIDS-typed dataset linked to a "Record EEG" task tells both *what* was collected and *how*.

**Provenance and packaging.** RO-Crate packages research artifacts with metadata for FAIR exchange, and Workflow Run RO-Crate records computational workflow executions [@soilandreyes2022rocrate; @leo2024wfrunrocrate]. These describe retrospectively; Studyflow specifies prospectively and executably, and what its runs record is *behavioral* provenance, the actor, observation, decision, response, and outcome of human and artificial subjects alike, not only the computational graph. The natural interface is packaging a study's `.studyflow` file, exported figure, and shared trials table as an RO-Crate for deposit, which is how this article's worked example is archived.

**Reporting guidelines.** CONSORT, SPIRIT, STROBE, and STARD enforce structure at the publication stage [@moher2012; @spirit2013; @strobe; @stard]; authored as Studyflow, a guideline carries its checklist items as elements, so conformance becomes a property the diagram can be checked for rather than a manual audit of PDF supplements.

**Other BPMN profiles.** BPMN4CP for clinical pathways [@braun2014], BPMN4sML for serverless ML [@tetzlaff2022bpmn4sml], and the human and agent extension [@ait2024bpmn_humanagent] are sibling profiles in adjacent domains, and Studyflow's architecture follows the same pattern. Visual modeling languages already used in life sciences, such as Systems Biology Graphical Notation [@novere2009], confirm both the appetite for graphical formalization and the importance of domain-specific vocabulary [@norouzi2025semantic_processes]. Studyflow also does not aim to be an ontology of experimental design. Process ontologies are numerous but tend to have high upfront cost and low reuse [@norouzi2025semantic_processes], so we have kept the profile small and enforced by tooling rather than by manual inspection.

A shared architectural pattern across several adjacent systems makes Studyflow's position concrete. LinkML [@moxon2025linkml], NIDM Results [@maumet2016nidm], BIDS [@bids], ISA-Tab [@sansone2012isa], RO-Crate [@soilandreyes2022rocrate], and ARTEM-IS [@styles2021artemis; @soskic2025artemis] share one architecture but occupy *different planes*: a schema layer, a human-friendly authoring layer, and machine-readable outputs, applied respectively to the data model, analysis outputs, data organization, experiment metadata, packaging, and methods reporting. The procedural plane of this architecture, a machine-readable, human-authorable specification of the study *process*, is the gap that Studyflow fills. ARTEM-IS is the closest existing precedent in spirit: it commits the EEG methods reporting community to structured templates that emit both human-readable forms and JSON. Studyflow generalizes the same commitment, from EEG methods reporting to whole procedural specification.

## Objections and alternate views

A profile that spans protocol, execution, analysis, and publication invites objections from both audiences, and we take the strongest ones in turn rather than wait for them at review. Each is stated as a skeptic would state it, and each answer concedes what is true before saying what is left standing.

**"BPMN is heavyweight, and this is one more notation to learn."** This is a fair cost, and we do not claim it away. A reader new to flowcharts still faces a learning curve, gentler than a custom language would impose, because BPMN's visual grammar is already recognized across engineering and analysis [@white2004introduction; @moody2009physics]. We also keep the surface small, a mitigation backed by evidence since comprehension of process models degrades with size and connector count [@reijers2011understandability]: the layers that always load are the language core and a companion cognitive layer, and everything else is an optional domain layer a study never has to open (Table S1). The bet is that one worked example and a glossary are enough to start.

**"This is just a flowchart with extra labels."** A box-and-arrow figure communicates at a glance, and Studyflow keeps that affordance. The difference is that the same artifact is executable rather than only descriptive (R2): a runner walks the file a reviewer reads, stable identifiers let it diff in Git and embed in an SVG export (R1), and the elements validate against a versioned LinkML schema, so *cognitive task*, *random gateway*, and *eligibility check* carry checkable meaning rather than informal labels [@moxon2025linkml]. A flowchart that an ethics board reads, a participant runs, and a figure exports from one source is doing more than a flowchart.

**"Reading artificial agents as co-subjects in a CONSORT-style study overclaims; CONSORT is for human trials."** We agree that CONSORT was written for human randomized trials, and we do not assert that an agent cohort inherits the ethical or inferential standing of a human cohort. The skeptic's case is well documented: language models are not substitute humans, treating their data as human evidence carries interpretive fallacies, and AI surrogates risk illusions of understanding [@dillion2023replace; @lin2025fallacies; @messeri2024illusions]; clinical research has so far engaged AI from the inverse direction, as the intervention applied to patients rather than as a subject [@liu2020consortai; @cruzrivera2020spiritai]. The claim stays at the level of notation, in agreement with those critiques rather than against them: the enroll, allocate, run, and analyze topology is one shape, and because the executor is a runtime decision (R7), the same shape can route a human cohort and an agent cohort into one shared, schema validated table. For agents the scores are operational task performance; whether the tasks measure the same constructs in agents as in humans is itself an open question the shared protocol makes testable [@bean2025construct]. An auditable record of exactly what was administered is a precondition for taking the critiques seriously, not a verdict on agent standing, which remains a question for the ethics and evaluation literatures.

**"A single source of truth is brittle and risks tool lock-in."** A single source does concentrate risk, and the design answers that directly. The core specification is a LinkML schema maintained separately from the modeler (R6), and the artifact on disk is plain BPMN 2.0 XML that opens in any compliant tool and degrades gracefully when a tool does not know the domain extensions (R4) [@white2004introduction; @magnani2009bpdmn]. The modeler is one open-source client of that schema, so a project that abandons our tooling keeps a valid file that no single tool owns. We treat the concentration as the feature and the independence from any single tool as the safeguard.

## Limitations

The scope limits of the current system fall into two kinds, and we keep them apart because conflating them would misstate what the language can express. The first kind is a choice of scope in the *tooling*, where the diagram is fully expressive at modeling time and each gap corresponds to a roadmap item. The Studyflow Runner ships a fixed set of step kinds, does not support parallel gateways, falls back to a uniform pick where balanced or blocked allocation is called for (so small samples can realize unbalanced arms), has no counterbalancing primitive beyond seeded order randomization, and does not yet traverse choreography tasks. The multi-actor setup likewise works today for the Behaverse battery, the 22 tasks recognized by our data server, CogEnv, CogPonder, and the runner; a custom PsychoPy [@peirce2019psychopy] or jsPsych [@deleeuw2015jspsych] task referenced from a diagram still runs for human participants, but the reinforcement learning, recurrent-model, and language model adapters would each need a matching bridge to read its stimulus stream and inject responses. None of these is a limit of the notation, and generalizing the trial-level interface beyond this battery is a roadmap item.

The second kind is a deliberate boundary of *what Studyflow is for* rather than a missing feature. Studyflow is a specification of the study process and not a stimulus presentation library, so rendering letters at a fixed retinal angle still requires the assessment battery itself or an external framework reached by URL; the diagram describes which stimulus to show, in what order, under what timing constraint, and what to record, and the pixel-level mechanics, including the millisecond timing precision that browser collection bounds [@bridges2020timing; @anwylirvine2021timing], are left to the presentation software and characterized there; the latency readouts in this study are medians over many trials, coarse enough that browser jitter is immaterial. Some designs are also intrinsically awkward to express as directed graphs, including adaptive trials, certain Bayesian sequential designs, and ABAB single-subject designs that need feedback, dynamic re-allocation, or open-ended replay; the choreography and message-flow elements reach some of this, and the rest is current research. A notation also does not solve the measurement problems AI evaluation has named: train-test contamination [@xu2024contamination], prompt sensitivity [@biderman2024lessons], and construct validity [@bean2025construct] survive an auditable protocol; what the protocol adds is a record of exactly what was administered, which any such audit presupposes. For the commercial language model, reproducibility is bounded by provider availability: the run pins the provider's snapshot identifier, while the open-weight arm replicates fully offline.

Two claims central to the paper remain unvalidated, and we mark them as such. We have not measured the legibility of large process-plus-data diagrams against the protocol PDFs, manuscript flow figures, and analysis scripts they replace; classic comparisons of flowcharts against text found advantages in some studies and none in others [@scanlan1989flowcharts; @shneiderman1977flowcharts], so the single-source comprehension benefit (R3) is a design goal awaiting a usability study, for which the process-model comprehension literature supplies validated measures and designs [@figl2017comprehension]. Adoption is also limited: the tooling ships under the MIT license and runs in the browser, but external uptake is a goal, not a result. Naming these edges is part of the contribution.

## Future directions

The nearest-term direction is community extension. Sibling BPMN extensions in clinical pathways and other domains emerged because a small number of groups committed to the same notation, and Studyflow's layered design is deliberately set up to make new domain extensions cheap, each one being a single schema file plus optional rendering code. The adoption signals we watch for are concrete: domain schemas authored outside our group, studies modeled by labs we have not met, and reporting-guideline templates contributed upstream.

Two lines of empirical work would strengthen the evidence base. The first is a usability study with cognitive scientists, comparing Studyflow diagrams against the artifacts they replace to test whether the design measurably reduces effort and error. The second is a set of demonstrations beyond the single study here: a multi-session longitudinal study, a test-retest design, an MLOps pipeline with an audit and training loop, and a larger human and agent benchmark. On the AI side, the natural next step is a bridge that compiles the agent branch of a `.studyflow` protocol into an Inspect or lm-eval task [@aisi2024inspect; @biderman2024lessons], so the same registrable protocol that enrolls a human cohort also ships as a standard eval the existing harness ecosystem can run; a Studyflow-specified battery is likewise directly consumable by foundation models of cognition trained on standardized protocol corpora [@binz2025centaur]. On the same path, the pinned executor configuration (model identity and version, sampling parameters, trait prompt, context policy) is a model card in all but type [@mitchell2019modelcards]; promoting those records to typed slots on the Actor element would make agent provenance a contract the validator checks, as dataset bindings already are. The case for the machine-readable protocol itself only grows as discovery moves toward multi-agent laboratories and language models act as both experimenter and subject [@ghareeb2025; @manning2024automated], and alignment research makes the same case from the measurement side [@nayebi2026alignment].

More broadly, experimental science increasingly runs on large datasets and automated pipelines, yet the process that produces a result still lacks the machine-readable footing the data already has. Studyflow is one attempt to give it that footing, a candidate process-level counterpart to what BIDS gave the data: a study read, run, and trusted from a single source, rather than a trail of documents about it.

# Materials and methods

This section gives the implementation and specification detail behind the framework: the layered schema that defines the language, the formal grammar, the serialization on disk, the executor interface and execution semantics, the conventions that make a run reproducible, and the human participants of the worked study. A Key Resources Table listing the toolkit components, schemas, models, and deposits with their identifiers accompanies this section [FILL: MDAR Key Resources Table with RRIDs and DOIs].

## The language specification

The Studyflow language is defined once and projected into the format each tool needs. The normative definition of the core is a versioned LinkML schema [@moxon2025linkml] that fixes the element types, attribute constraints, and validation rules independently of any tool; the canonical copy lives in the standalone schemas repository, tagged by version, and the copy bundled with the modeler is a pinned snapshot of it. Its header declares the prefixes that bind Studyflow to the host standard and the community data models: `bpmn` for the BPMN metamodel, `studyflow` and `cognitive` for the two core layers, and `bids`, `psychds`, `bdm`, and `csvw` for the data bindings. Keeping the specification in LinkML rather than in the modeler codebase is what makes the notation independent of any tool.

The runtime tooling reads a mirror of that source in the format the BPMN engine expects: the browser's BPMN library consumes moddle YAML schemas, so each core LinkML definition is mirrored into a moddle layer carrying the same element types and attributes; the mirrors are checked against the LinkML source, with mechanical generation on the roadmap [FILL: confirm the current discipline]. The vocabulary is partitioned into six layers, which the modeler discovers at startup, always loading the two core layers. The core layers are `studyflow` (the study container, events, sequence flows, the base activity, and shared data infrastructure) and its companion `cognitive` layer (cognitive tasks, video game paradigms, rest periods, questionnaires, instructions, and research gateways). Four optional layers load on demand: a Behaverse cognitive assessment battery, a process-orchestration library, a data transformation library for large datasets, and a multimodal acquisition layer for EEG and eye-tracking hardware. The core layers are LinkML-defined and independent of any tool; the four optional layers are currently specified at the moddle level, with LinkML promotion on the roadmap.

The schemas drive everything downstream, so documentation, validator, and converters are derived rather than hand-maintained. The element catalog of @tbl-elements and Supplementary Table S1 is generated from the same LinkML source, and the modeler can emit a LinkML instance from a diagram's data elements, each class tied back to its Studyflow type. Because one schema generates the interface, the documentation, and the validation, adding an element type or attribute updates all three at once.

## The Studyflow grammar

The structural shape of a Studyflow diagram can also be stated as a reference abstract syntax, independent of the file format in which it is stored. The grammar is non-normative: well-formedness is defined by validation against the versioned schema plus the structural constraints (Formal definition); Supplementary Listing S1 restates a representative subset of the extension vocabulary in a form useful to third-party parser writers. Inherited BPMN constructs (timer and error event definitions, pools, message flows outside choreography) follow the OMG grammar [@bpmnspec] and are abbreviated here.


## Serialization

A Studyflow file on disk is a valid BPMN 2.0 XML document in which every element is a standard BPMN element whose payload resides in an `extensionElements` block, so the structure a generic BPMN tool expects is untouched.

This extension mechanism is what makes compatibility a property of the format rather than a feature of any one reader. A generic BPMN reader ignores the extension content it does not recognize and still draws a correct process diagram, while a supported tool reads, validates, and renders the extension blocks. This is BPMN's standard extension protocol [@stroppi2011], so each reader interprets the elements it cares about. The study root marks itself with a `studyflow:study` element inside the root process's `extensionElements`, which lets a validating tool recognize the file as a study without changing how a generic tool treats the underlying `bpmn:process`.

Two further serialization conventions support the design goals. First, Studyflow leaves XML namespaces, element identifiers, and the base vocabulary untouched, so a diagram produces clean line-based diffs in Git and stays valid BPMN. Second, the canonical serialization of a study is the `.studyflow` XML file; the `.studyflow.svg` publication export is a carrier that embeds that XML losslessly in the SVG metadata, and the embedded XML, not the rendering, is normative. *Round trip.* Extraction reproduces the source file, a property enforced by a round-trip test in the modeler [FILL: confirm], so the figure a reader downloads from an author's own hosted or deposited SVG is the runnable study itself.

## The executor interface and execution semantics

The runner administers every actor through one message passing interface. Per trial it sends an observation (the stimulus, the allowed responses, the timing constraint, and where needed a rendered frame at a declared resolution) and receives a response and, where the actor produces one behaviorally, a response time. An actor is anything that implements this function from observations to responses; humans, reinforcement learning policies, recurrent models, and language models are instances of one abstraction, which is what makes the protocol executor agnostic (R7).

Execution itself is a deterministic walk. A run of a well-formed file $F$ with study seed $s$, subject identifier $i$, and actor $a$ is a sequence of configurations (current node, pseudorandom-number-generator state, opaque actor state). Control is a single token: the runner advances along the unique enabled outgoing flow; at a typed gateway the branch is chosen by the gateway's rule, with randomness drawn from that subject's generator; activities emit an observation to the actor and consume its response, or its recorded timeout, as external input, and the runner's flag counts are part of the configuration. Two properties of this semantics are the contract a third-party executor must preserve (the conformance levels of the toolkit section), so we name them. *Determinism.* For fixed $(F, s, i)$, the visited node sequence is a function of the input sequence (responses and timeouts) alone, so the protocol any subject encountered is exactly reconstructable from the file, the study seed, and the subject identifier. *Amendment stability.* Random draws use separate substreams keyed by stable element identifiers, so inserting a node upstream does not perturb the draws of unaffected downstream elements; a protocol amendment leaves the draws of untouched elements bit identical at the same study seed. The runner implements this semantics for the executable subset of the language (exclusive-family gateways, boundary timer and error events); inherited BPMN constructs outside the subset, parallel gateways and choreography among them, validate but do not yet run.

## Reproducibility

The seed policy separates what is fixed from what is sampled. The study seed combined with the subject identifier derives a seed for each subject that fixes path allocation, task order, stimulus order within each task, and every random branch; seeds are generated and recorded by the study runner rather than typed by the subject, and the seed log is part of the run record [FILL: confirm allocation concealment mechanics for the human arm]. Responses are sampled, not seeded: human behavior is human behavior, and language model responses are draws under recorded sampling parameters. Every agent run pins the executor configuration as part of its enrollment record: model identifier and version (a content digest and quantization level for open-weight models, a provider snapshot identifier for the commercial model), sampling parameters, the versioned trait prompt, the context policy (whether and how context accumulates across trials and tasks, and the truncation behavior), and the frame resolution for vision input. Per trial, the record stores the observation sent, the raw reply, the parsed response, the flag and failure mode where parsing failed, and the latency with its provenance class. The trials table is therefore the run's complete behavioral trace, and reproducing the agent arm requires only the `.studyflow` file, the seed log, and the pinned executor configurations; the commercial arm is additionally bounded by provider availability of the pinned snapshot.

## Human participants

Nine adult volunteers completed the battery in the runner [FILL: recruitment channel, age and gender summary, compensation, session duration]. The sample was sized as a feasibility demonstration of the framework, not to power human comparisons between arms. The study was approved by the Ethics Review Panel of the University of Luxembourg [FILL: approval number and date, which must precede the runs]; all participants gave written informed consent through the consent screen rendered from the protocol's start event, the same consent document referenced by the file's `consentFormUri`. The approval reference is recorded in the deposited file itself [FILL: confirm, else delete], so the compliance trail is auditable from the artifact that ran the study. Human trial data are shared only in de-identified form (Data availability); screening collected demographics only, no special-category data were gathered or shared, and demographics are reported in aggregate only and excluded from the released trials table.

## Ethics and responsible use

The artificial agents in this study were used in an evaluation-only capacity: they performed standard cognitive tasks under a fixed protocol, with no fine-tuning, no autonomous tool use, and no capability elicitation beyond the published battery. *Co-subject* is a notational convenience about shared protocol topology, not a claim of moral or inferential standing. Studyflow supports but does not replace ethics review, guideline conformance decisions, or recruitment; a human board reviews and decides. Model identities, versions, sampling parameters, and trait prompts are pinned per run in the shared dataset, so every agent result is auditable from the same artifact that ran it. The commercial model was accessed through its public API under the provider's terms of service; model outputs in the released dataset are distributed consistent with each provider's terms. [FILL: AI usage disclosure per eLife policy, covering both content generation and writing or editing assistance.]

# Data availability

All artifacts are open source under the MIT license and run in the browser without installation. The modeler, runner, and corresponding documentation are hosted at [behaverse.org/studyflow-modeler/app](https://behaverse.org/studyflow-modeler/app), and the source code is available at [github.com/behaverse/studyflow-modeler](https://github.com/behaverse/studyflow-modeler). The canonical schema is versioned separately at [github.com/behaverse/schemas](https://github.com/behaverse/schemas). Archived releases of the modeler, runner, and schemas, tagged by version, are deposited with DOIs [FILL: Zenodo DOIs], and the versions used in this paper are tagged in the repositories.

The worked example is archived as a research-object package [FILL: deposit DOI] containing the registered `.studyflow` protocol, the exported figure SVGs with embedded sources, the de-identified human trials table and the complete agent trials table (one BDM and Psych-DS compatible schema for both populations), the seed log, the pinned executor configurations including the versioned trait prompts, and RO-Crate metadata [@soilandreyes2022rocrate]. Example diagrams referenced in the paper ship with the modeler: a CONSORT 2025-style randomized trial, a SPIRIT 2025 schedule of enrolment and assessment, a base demo, and three agent profiling demos (`bot_external.studyflow`, a randomized baseline; `bot_claude.studyflow`, a commercial language model; and `bot_ollama.studyflow`, a local open-weight model). Every figure is reproducible by opening the corresponding diagram in the hosted modeler and exporting SVG; runner figures are reproduced by loading the same files into the runner at study seed 42.

# Figure captions

**Figure 1. The process plane has no shared artifact.** Schematic of a study's lifecycle across its audiences (researcher, ethics board, participant, engineer, analyst, reviewer, replicator), with the artifact each works from (protocol PDF, ethics application, experiment script, analysis notebook, manuscript figure, flow diagram) and the families of existing tools mapped onto the slice of the lifecycle each covers. The diagram highlights the gap the paper addresses: no single representation spans the full lifecycle in a form every audience can read, validate, and execute.

**Figure 2. The layered schema architecture.** The two core layers that always load (the language scaffolding and the cognitive layer) and the four optional domain layers (cognitive assessment battery, process orchestration, data transformation, multimodal acquisition), with the LinkML source generating the runtime schemas, the validator, the documentation, and the element catalog. New domains plug in as additional layers without changing the core.

**Figure 3. The Studyflow modeler.** Annotated screenshot of the schema-driven modeler: the palette and inspector generated from the layered schemas, validation feedback, the simulation mode stepping through gateway logic, and the export and publish actions. [FILL: screenshot from the released modeler version.]

**Figure 4. The runner walks the diagram a participant sees.** Side-by-side panels pairing nodes of the worked study's diagram with the participant-facing screens the runner renders for them: consent (start event), an instruction, a questionnaire, one n-back trial, and the completion screen. [FILL: runner screenshots from the seed-42 walkthrough.]

**Figure 5. Four views of one source.** The same `.studyflow` file projected as the Study view (structural graph), the Gantt view (temporal attributes on a time axis), the Checklist view (flattened items with status), and the Figure view (curated publication export). Edits to the source propagate to every view; no view is edited independently.

**Figure 6. CONSORT flow as a Studyflow diagram.** (a) The CONSORT 2025 reference participant-flow diagram, redrawn [FILL: confirm CC BY-licensed source for the reference panel]. (b) The Studyflow encoding with the same labels and pathways. (c) Annotated contrast: attrition as boundary error events wired to counted error end events (left path) versus the traditional unconnected side annotations (right path). The encoding makes the flow arithmetic a checkable conservation law: at every activity, inflow equals outflow plus attrition. Counts in (b) are checked by the validator against this law; counts in (a), as in any published flow diagram, are maintained by hand.

**Figure 7. Encoding n-back trials.** A traditional slide version of the n-back figure (left) next to the Studyflow encoding (right): the trial as an explicit subgraph with a stimulus activity, a boundary timer for the response window, a second timer for the inter-trial interval, and labeled target and non-target branches; below, the compressed form, a single cognitive task whose inline configuration the runner expands into trials (Listing 2).

**Figure 8. One executor, many actors.** The message passing executor interface: per trial, the runner sends an observation (stimulus, allowed responses, timing constraint, optional rendered frame) and records a response, with four actor families behind the interface (human participant, reinforcement learning agent via CogEnv, recurrent cognitive model via CogPonder, language model with versioned trait prompt). Actor state stays opaque to the runner; flagged replies and the attrition rule on whole runs route failures to the participant flow's boundary error events.

**Figure 9. Human and agent profiles across the battery.** Accuracy (and, for actor families with interpretable latencies, response time) per task for every model and trait cell at study seed 42, faceted by RT provenance class, with the nine human participants as a reference band and the uniform random baseline at chance. [FILL: rendered from the seed-42 runs.]

**Figure 10. The analysis pipeline is the preregistration.** Left: the RT analysis subprocess as a typed Studyflow pipeline (read, filter with the shared exclusion rules, map to derived measures, a reduce in two stages, first to subject summaries and then to group statistics, the typed equivalence test node carrying its margin and alpha, manual outlier review, schema-declared outputs). Right: the equivalent dplyr implementation. Divergence between the two surfaces as a graph diff in the data operation markers and the input and output schemas.


**Figure 11. SPIRIT as plan, CONSORT as report, one file.** The worked study rendered three ways from one source: the SPIRIT 2025 schedule of enrolment and assessment as a Gantt view, the checklist audit of SPIRIT items, and the CONSORT flow with attrition counts written into the boundary error events after the run. The registered file and the file as run differ only in those counts (Listing 3).

# Supplementary materials

## Listing S1. The Studyflow grammar

**Listing S1.** A reference abstract syntax for the Studyflow extension vocabulary, in EBNF notation. A study is a labeled collection of elements, sequence flows, and data associations; activity and gateway types; data operations; data elements; and choreography constructs.

```ebnf
/* ========== Top level ========== */
Definitions       ::= Study
Study             ::= 'Study' Identifier Attribute* (Element | SequenceFlow | DataAssociation)*
SubProcess        ::= 'SubProcess' Identifier Attribute* (Element | SequenceFlow | DataAssociation)*
Element           ::= Event | Activity | Gateway | SubProcess | Actor
                    | DataObject | DataCatalog | DataStorage | Dataset
                    | Schema | Array | Snapshot

/* ========== Events ========== */
Event             ::= StartEvent | EndEvent | BoundaryEvent
StartEvent        ::= 'StartEvent' Identifier Attribute*    /* may carry consentFormUri */
EndEvent          ::= 'EndEvent' Identifier Attribute*      /* may carry redirectTo, completionCodeType,
                                                               completionCode, errorRef, count */
BoundaryEvent     ::= 'BoundaryEvent' Identifier Attribute* /* attachedToRef; timer or error definition */
Actor             ::= 'Actor' Identifier Attribute*         /* actorType: human | LLM | agent | instrument;
                                                               serialized at the collaboration level */

/* ========== Activities ========== */
Activity              ::= 'Activity' Identifier ActivityAttributeList Choreography?
ActivityAttributeList ::= ActivityType ActivityAttribute*
ActivityType          ::= '@type' ('CognitiveTask' | 'Questionnaire' | 'Instruction' |
                                   'Rest' | 'VideoGame' | 'BehaverseTask' |
                                   'Script' | 'Manual')
ActivityAttribute     ::= Attribute | DataInput | DataOutput | DataOperation

/* ========== Data transformations ========== */
DataOperation      ::= OpClause+
OpClause           ::= '@op' (PrimitiveOp | CompositeOp) DataInput+ DataOutput+
PrimitiveOp        ::= 'Transform' | 'Map' | 'Filter' | 'FlatMap' | 'Reduce' | 'Group'
CompositeOp        ::= 'Compose' PrimitiveOp+

/* ========== Data elements ========== */
DataCatalog        ::= 'DataCatalog' Identifier Attribute*               /* url */
DataStorage        ::= 'DataStorage' Identifier Attribute*               /* persistent physical store */
Dataset            ::= 'Dataset' Identifier Attribute*                   /* catalog, storage, schema, format */
Schema             ::= 'Schema' Identifier Attribute*                    /* format, body */
Array              ::= 'Array' Identifier Attribute*                     /* dataset, schema */
Snapshot           ::= 'Snapshot' Identifier Attribute*                  /* source, version */
DataObject         ::= 'DataObject' Identifier Attribute*                /* may carry state */
DataInput          ::= '@in' NodeRef
DataOutput         ::= '@out' NodeRef

/* ========== Choreography ========== */
Choreography     ::= 'Choreography' Attribute* ParticipantRef ParticipantRef+ InitiatingParticipant MessageFlowList
ParticipantRef   ::= ProcessRef
InitiatingParticipant ::= ParticipantRef
MessageFlowList  ::= MessageFlow*
MessageFlow      ::= 'MessageFlow' Identifier Attribute* ParticipantRef '->' ParticipantRef

/* ========== Gateways ========== */
Gateway          ::= 'Gateway' Identifier GatewayAttribute*
GatewayAttribute ::= GatewayType | Attribute
GatewayType      ::= '@type' ('Random' | 'StratifiedAllocation' | 'Eligibility' |
                              'Exclusive' | 'Parallel' | 'Inclusive' | 'Complex')
SequenceFlow     ::= 'SequenceFlow' Identifier Attribute* NodeRef '->' NodeRef
                                                            /* optional conditionExpression */
DataAssociation  ::= 'DataAssociation' Identifier NodeRef '->' NodeRef

/* ========== Common definitions ========== */
Attribute             ::= Identifier Value
ProcessRef            ::= Identifier
NodeRef               ::= Identifier

/* ========== Basic value types ========== */
Boolean    ::= 'true' | 'false'
Value      ::= String | Number | Boolean | Identifier
Number     ::= '-'? ( [0-9]+ ('.' [0-9]*)? | '.' [0-9]+ )
String     ::= '"' [^"]* '"'
Identifier ::= [A-Za-z] [A-Za-z0-9_]*
```

## Listing S2. Research gateways in the runtime schema

**Listing S2.** Two research gateways, each a specialization of `bpmn:ExclusiveGateway` (runtime schema excerpt; abridged). The diagram stays valid BPMN while the extension carries the randomization and eligibility semantics.

```yaml
- name: RandomGateway
  superClass:
    - bpmn:ExclusiveGateway
    - bpmn:BaseElement
  properties:
    - name: algorithm
      type: AssignmentAlgorithmEnum
      default: probabilistic
    - name: probabilityFunction
      type: String
      default: uniform
- name: EligibilityGateway
  superClass:
    - bpmn:ExclusiveGateway
    - bpmn:BaseElement
  properties:
    - name: inclusionCriteria
      type: MarkdownString
      isMany: true
    - name: exclusionCriteria
      type: MarkdownString
      isMany: true
```

## Figure S1. Multimodal pipeline

**Figure S1. A multimodal preprocessing and training pipeline in the same notation.** Specification (not executed here) of a pipeline harmonizing EEG, eye-tracking, and behavioral recordings across heterogeneous public datasets into BDM trials, with explicit multiverse branches, provenance traced through the nodes, and downstream training and evaluation subprocesses sharing the notation of the behavioral analysis.

## Table S1. The Studyflow element catalog

The catalog below lists the elements of the two core layers (the language core and the companion cognitive layer). Every element specializes a standard BPMN type, given in the *BPMN base* column, so a diagram remains valid BPMN 2.0 and degrades gracefully in a generic BPMN tool. Four optional domain layers (a cognitive assessment battery, a generic process orchestration layer, a data transformation layer for large datasets, and a multimodal acquisition layer for EEG and eye tracking) add further specialized elements that plug in without changing the core. The element types, their attributes, and validation rules are generated from the versioned LinkML schema, which is the authoritative source.

- - **Core layer**

Every element also inherits `documentation` and `checklist` attributes from a shared `Element` mixin. The catalog additionally defines enumerations used by these attributes, including dataset formats (BDM, BIDS, Psych-DS, CSVW), BDM data levels, completion-code types, runtimes, assignment algorithms, and instrument identifiers.
